subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on lever systems, planes and axes of movement, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain lever systems, planes and axes of movement for GCSE PE simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: In a first-class lever, which component is positioned in the middle, between the effort and the load?
questions.explain: In a first-class lever the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load (order E-F-L), like a seesaw. An example is the neck nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint.

questions.q: Standing up onto tiptoes (plantarflexion at the ankle) is an example of which class of lever?
questions.explain: Rising onto tiptoes is a second-class lever: the fulcrum is the ball of the foot, the load (body weight) is in the middle, and the effort (calf muscles via the Achilles) is at the heel. Order is F-L-E.

questions.q: Which class of lever always has the effort positioned between the fulcrum and the load?
questions.explain: A third-class lever has the effort in the middle (order F-E-L). A biceps curl is a classic example, with the elbow as the fulcrum, the biceps as the effort, and the forearm/weight as the load.

questions.q: Why do second-class levers provide a large mechanical advantage?
options: The effort arm is longer than the load arm
The fulcrum is exactly in the middle
The load arm is longer than the effort arm
questions.explain: Mechanical advantage = effort arm divided by load arm. In a second-class lever the effort arm is longer than the load arm, so a small effort can move a large load.

questions.q: A biceps curl uses a third-class lever. What is the main trade-off compared with a second-class lever?
options: It cannot move any load at all
The fulcrum must be in the middle
It has a mechanical advantage below 1, favouring range and speed of movement
It gains a very large mechanical advantage
questions.explain: In a third-class lever the load arm is longer than the effort arm, giving a mechanical advantage less than 1. It sacrifices force for greater range and speed of movement.

questions.q: In any lever system, which structure of the body acts as the fulcrum?
questions.explain: The joint acts as the fulcrum (pivot). Muscles provide the effort, and the load is the weight of the body part or resistance being moved.

questions.q: Which plane divides the body into left and right halves?
questions.explain: The sagittal plane divides the body into left and right. Movements such as flexion and extension (e.g. a somersault or biceps curl) occur in this plane.

questions.q: Which plane divides the body into front and back halves?
questions.explain: The frontal plane divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior). Abduction and adduction, such as a star jump or cartwheel, occur in the frontal plane.

questions.q: The transverse plane divides the body into which two parts?
questions.explain: The transverse plane divides the body into top (superior) and bottom (inferior) halves. Rotation movements, such as a full twist in trampolining, occur in this plane.

questions.q: A gymnast performing a forward somersault rotates about which axis?
questions.explain: A somersault is flexion/extension in the sagittal plane, rotating about the transverse (frontal) axis, which runs from left to right through the body.

questions.q: An ice skater performing a spin rotates about which axis?
questions.explain: A spin is rotation in the transverse plane about the longitudinal (vertical) axis, which runs top to bottom through the centre of the body.

questions.q: A cartwheel involves abduction and adduction. Which axis does the body rotate about?
questions.explain: A cartwheel occurs in the frontal plane and rotates about the sagittal axis, which runs from front to back through the body.

questions.q: During the upward (lifting) phase of a biceps curl, the biceps performs which type of contraction?
questions.explain: As the muscle shortens under tension while lifting the weight, it performs an isotonic concentric contraction.

questions.q: Lowering a weight slowly during the downward phase of a biceps curl is an example of which contraction?
questions.explain: During controlled lowering the muscle lengthens while still under tension, which is an isotonic eccentric contraction. This is often where muscle soreness develops.

questions.q: Holding a plank position steady is an example of which type of muscle contraction?
questions.explain: Holding a plank means the muscle is under tension but its length does not change, so it is an isometric contraction.

questions.q: Which pair of movements occurs at the ankle?
questions.explain: The ankle performs plantarflexion (pointing the toes down) and dorsiflexion (pulling the toes up towards the shin).

questions.q: Raising the arm sideways away from the midline of the body is called...
questions.explain: Abduction moves a limb away from the body's midline. Adduction is the return movement back towards the midline (add = 'adds to' the body).

questions.q: Bending the knee to reduce the angle at the joint is an example of...
questions.explain: Flexion decreases the angle at a joint (bending); extension increases the angle (straightening). Bending the knee is flexion.

questions.q: In an antagonistic muscle pair, what are the roles of the two muscles during a movement?
options: Both contract at the same time
One is the agonist (prime mover) contracting while the other is the antagonist relaxing
questions.explain: In an antagonistic pair one muscle (the agonist/prime mover) contracts to create the movement while the other (the antagonist) relaxes to allow it.

questions.q: During the upward phase of a biceps curl, which muscle is the agonist and which is the antagonist?
questions.explain: During flexion in a biceps curl the biceps is the agonist (contracting) and the triceps is the antagonist (relaxing). The roles reverse during extension.
